title: Yet the first act of conversion is vital and free
source_text: XXII. Neque tamen vel ille vel alii Reformati negant propterea primum conversionis actum esse actum vitalem, & actionem a facultate illa, quae voluntas in nobis dicitur, elicitam: imo non inficiantur esse actionem liberam, & ex earum numero quae in Scholis humanae vocantur. Hoc solum sibi volunt; quum Deus hominem convertit, primum illud quod gratia in nobis operatur quiddam esse quod liberam hominis motionem ad bonum omnino praevenit. Adeoque non videntur hac in parte Reformati a sanioribus inter Scholasticos dissentire, licet aliis verbis mentem suam exprimant.
pass_a_gloss: XXII. Nor yet does either he or other Reformed deny on that account that the first act of conversion is a vital act, and an action elicited from that faculty, which is called the will in us: nay they do not deny that it is a free action, and of the number of those which in the Schools are called human. This only they mean; when God converts man, that first thing which grace works in us is something which wholly goes before the free motion of man toward good. And so in this part the Reformed do not seem to dissent from the sounder among the Scholastics, although they express their mind in other words.
pass_b_english: Thesis XXII. Still, neither he nor the other Reformed deny on this account that the first act of conversion is a vital act, an action produced by the faculty in us called the will. Indeed they do not deny that it is a free action and one of those the schools call human acts.

Their only point is this: when God converts a person, the first thing grace works in us is something that goes entirely before the person's free movement toward good. On this point, then, the Reformed seem not to differ from the sounder scholastics, though they put their meaning in other words.
